title: Ancient DNA Reveals Medieval Graves Weren't Family Burials
summary:
When archaeologists find an adult and a child buried in the same medieval grave, it's tempting to assume they were family. New research from Stockholm University, published in Science Advances, shows that assumption is usually wrong.

Scientists analyzed ancient DNA from 142 people who lived during the late Viking Age and Middle Ages in Sweden. The remains came from graves at Sigtuna, Västerhus, and Fjälkinge. More than 60 of the individuals were children and adolescents.

The genetic evidence revealed that close biological relatives were surprisingly uncommon among people placed in the same grave. This was true even in cemeteries where many biological family connections existed among the wider population.

"We often assume that adults and children sharing a grave were parents and children or other close family members," says Maja Krzewińska, lead author of the study. "In most cases, that was not what we found."

Instead, social, religious, or community ties may have decided who was buried together. "Ancient DNA has finally given us the tool we have been waiting for to test these interpretations directly," says Anna Kjellström, a researcher at Stockholm University.

The DNA also let scientists determine the biological sex of children whose bones were too young to identify reliably. At Västerhus, men and women were generally buried on different sides of the churchyard — and boys and girls followed the same pattern. "The children were not treated as a separate category," says Anders Götherström, professor of molecular archaeology.

One individual stood out. Lady 56, buried at Västerhus, was linked by DNA to her parents, her brother, and two daughters. She was buried with a scallop shell — a symbol of pilgrimage to Santiago de Compostela in northwestern Spain. Its presence suggests she may have completed one of medieval Europe's most famous pilgrimages, traveling thousands of kilometers before returning home. She died before the age of 30.

The study shows how archaeogenetics can reveal far more than family relationships — it can help reconstruct how medieval communities were organized and how children were treated in life and death.
why_it_matters: Learning that medieval graves were organised by community rather than blood family challenges a habit we still have today — assuming that anyone who lives together or stays together must be related. It shows how science can overturn stories societies tell about their own past.

background_read: The graves in this study come from the late Viking Age and the Middle Ages — the centuries, roughly from 800 to 1500, when Scandinavia gradually changed from a pagan, seafaring society into Christian kingdoms.

Stockholm University, where the researchers work, is one of Sweden's largest public universities; the study appeared in Science Advances, a peer-reviewed journal published by the same organization that publishes the journal Science.

Sigtuna, one of the three sites, is a small Swedish town that was one of the country's earliest cities and an important trading centre in Viking times, so its graves are a rich source of evidence about ordinary people.

Santiago de Compostela is a city in Galicia, in northwestern Spain, where Christian tradition says the remains of the apostle St. James are kept; for more than a thousand years pilgrims have walked long 'Camino' routes to reach it, and the scallop shell is the journey's emblem.

Ancient DNA is genetic material recovered from bones and teeth that are centuries old. It survives only in tiny, broken fragments, so researchers need careful laboratory methods and computing power to read it.

perspectives.description: Ancient DNA finally lets researchers test interpretations directly instead of guessing from grave positions and grave goods. The results also suggest medieval communities buried and cared for children who were not their biological kin, which complicates the idea that only family mattered.

DNA can show who was related, but it cannot explain why people were buried together — social, religious or practical reasons remain guesses. Highlighting one dramatic case such as 'Lady 56' can also make a broad statistical result feel more sensational than the evidence supports.

Medieval churchyards were normally organised by parish, wealth and status rather than by household, so the finding fits what written records already imply. Read that way, it is less a surprise than a confirmation that the living arranged the dead according to community rules.

Researchers will want to repeat these tests on cemeteries across Europe and on earlier periods to see whether the pattern is local or widespread. As ancient DNA becomes cheaper, small rural graves may be studied as closely as famous ones.
